## Big idea

Same CRUD API as lecture 11, but data lives in **MySQL** through **Spring Data JPA**.

```text
Controller → Service → JpaRepository → Hibernate → MySQL
```

## What you add

| Piece | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` | JPA + Hibernate starter |
| MySQL driver | Talk to MySQL |
| `application.properties` | URL, user, password |
| `@Entity` | Java class ↔ table |
| `JpaRepository` | Ready-made save/find/delete methods |

## Properties (example)

```properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/productdb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=secret
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
```

**Never commit real passwords.** Use env vars when you can.

## Entity

```java
@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private double price;
    // getters/setters
}
```

## Repository

```java
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
}
```

You get `save`, `findById`, `findAll`, `deleteById` for free.

## Service change

Inject `ProductRepository` instead of a `List`. Call repository methods.

## Practice checklist

1. Create MySQL database `productdb`.
2. Add JPA + MySQL dependencies.
3. Convert model to `@Entity`.
4. Add `ProductRepository`.
5. Wire service → repository.
6. Hit the same REST endpoints; confirm rows in MySQL.

## Reasoning

- `ddl-auto=update` is handy for learning; use migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) in real apps.
- Repository interfaces keep data access thin and testable.
